content: Cigarette smoking significantly increases the risk of severe complications associated with oral contraceptive use, such as heart attacks, blood clots, and strokes. This risk is particularly elevated in women over the age of 35 and in those who smoke heavily (15 or more cigarettes per day). If you are using oral contraceptives, you should not smoke. Oral contraceptives, commonly referred to as birth control pills, are medications designed to prevent pregnancy. They contain two female sex hormones, estrogen and progestin, which work together to inhibit ovulation (the release of an egg from the ovaries). Additionally, these hormones alter the uterine lining to prevent implantation of a fertilized egg and thicken cervical mucus to block sperm from entering the uterus. While highly effective in preventing pregnancy, oral contraceptives do not protect against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. Certain brands of oral contraceptives are also prescribed to treat acne by reducing levels of specific natural substances that contribute to acne formation. Oral contraceptives are available in packets containing 21, 28, or 91 tablets. They are taken orally once daily, ideally at the same time each day, to maintain consistent hormone levels. To minimize nausea, it is recommended to take the pill with food or milk. Different brands of oral contraceptives may vary in their composition, dosing schedules, and associated risks and benefits. For 21-day packets, take one tablet daily for 21 days, followed by a 7-day break with no tablets. For 28-day packets, take one tablet daily for 28 days, including the last set of reminder tablets, which may not contain active ingredients but help maintain the habit of daily dosing. For 91-day packets, take one tablet daily for 91 days, following the order specified in the packet. The last set of tablets in these packets may contain either inactive ingredients or a low dose of estrogen. Always start a new packet immediately after finishing the previous one, regardless of whether you are still experiencing withdrawal bleeding. Your doctor will advise you on when to begin taking oral contraceptives, typically on the first or fifth day of your menstrual period or the first Sunday after bleeding begins. During the first 7 days of starting the medication, you may need to use an additional method of contraception. If you experience vomiting or diarrhea while taking oral contraceptives, consult your doctor, as this may reduce the pill's effectiveness, and you may need to use a backup contraceptive method. If you have recently given birth, wait at least 4 weeks postpartum before starting oral contraceptives. If you have had a miscarriage or abortion, consult your doctor about when to begin taking the medication. Oral contraceptives are effective only when taken consistently and as directed. Do not stop taking them without consulting your doctor, even if you experience side effects such as spotting, nausea, or other symptoms. In addition to preventing pregnancy, oral contraceptives may be prescribed for other medical conditions, such as heavy or irregular menstrual bleeding and endometriosis. These conditions should be discussed with your doctor to weigh the potential benefits and risks of using oral contraceptives for treatment. Before starting oral contraceptives, inform your doctor if you have any allergies to estrogen, progestin, or other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, supplements, and herbal products you are taking, as some may interact with oral contraceptives and reduce their effectiveness. Certain medical conditions, such as a history of blood clots, heart disease, stroke, liver disease, or certain cancers, may contraindicate the use of oral contraceptives. Inform your doctor of your medical history, including any family history of breast cancer or other relevant conditions. Do not take oral contraceptives if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you suspect you may be pregnant while taking oral contraceptives, contact your doctor immediately. If you miss a period while using a 91-day packet, or if you miss two consecutive periods with other types of packets, consult your doctor and use an alternative method of contraception until pregnancy is ruled out. If you are scheduled for surgery or dental procedures, inform your healthcare provider that you are taking oral contraceptives. Additionally, if you wear contact lenses and notice changes in your vision or discomfort, consult an eye doctor. Continue your normal diet unless otherwise instructed by your doctor. If you miss a dose of your oral contraceptive, follow the specific instructions provided with your medication. Missing doses may reduce the pill's effectiveness, and you may need to use a backup contraceptive method for 7 days or until the end of the cycle. Oral contraceptives may cause minor side effects, such as nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, bloating, diarrhea, constipation, changes in appetite, weight fluctuations, skin discoloration, acne, unusual hair growth, spotting, changes in menstrual flow, breast tenderness, or vaginal irritation. If these symptoms persist or worsen, inform your doctor. Severe side effects, though rare, require immediate medical attention. These include severe headaches, vomiting, speech difficulties, dizziness, numbness or weakness in the limbs, chest pain, coughing up blood, shortness of breath, vision changes, severe abdominal pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, unusual bleeding, or symptoms of depression. Oral contraceptives may increase the risk of liver tumors, breast or liver cancer, heart attacks, strokes, or blood clots. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Store oral contraceptives in their original packaging at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and out of reach of children. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Symptoms of overdose may include nausea and vaginal bleeding. Inform laboratory personnel that you are taking oral contraceptives before undergoing any tests. If you wish to stop taking oral contraceptives to become pregnant, consult your doctor, as it may take time for your menstrual cycle to normalize. Oral contraceptives may reduce folate levels, so discuss supplementation with your doctor if you plan to conceive soon after discontinuing the medication. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist with any questions about refills or usage.
